note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Assist in the provision of on the job training

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: On an electrical contracting site, what is the main job of a worker who assists with on-the-job training?
options: To sign the trainee's final certificate for the national qualification
To guide and support a trainee to learn the work safely and correctly
To do the trainee's tasks for them so that the job finishes on time
To check the trainee's time sheet and work out the wages each week

questions.stem: Who normally carries out the final, formal assessment of a trainee's competence for the qualification?
options: Any electrician on the crew who has worked beside the trainee
The client whose building the trainee helped to wire
The trainee, by filling in a self-check form
A qualified assessor who meets the training body's rules

questions.stem: Why is a person who helps with on-the-job training expected to set a good example on site?
options: Trainees copy what they see, including bad habits
It means the trainee will need no written instructions
It allows the trainer to skip the morning safety briefing
It lets the crew finish the job with no supervisor present

questions.stem: A new apprentice, Kemar, joins your crew. What should you find out first, before you plan his training?
options: Which football team he supports, so you can make friends
How much he is paid, to judge how hard to push him
What he can already do and what the job needs him to do
Whether he owns a van so that he can carry materials

questions.stem: Which document best shows the standard a trainee must reach in a task?
options: The unit of competency for that task
The trainee's school report from grade 9
The price list from the electrical supplier
The company's holiday rota for the year

questions.stem: A trainee bends PVC conduit well but makes untidy terminations at the distribution board. What does this tell you?
options: Train them again on everything from the start
Focus the next training on terminations
Stop training, as they will never be neat
Give them only conduit work from now on

questions.stem: Why ask a trainee how they learn best before the training starts?
options: So the trainee can choose which site rules to follow
So you can avoid teaching them the harder tasks
So all of the training can be finished in one day
So you can choose methods that help them to learn

questions.stem: What should a short on-the-job training plan for one task include?
options: Only the trainee's name and the date of the session
A list of every mistake the trainee has made so far
The aim, the steps, the resources and how it is checked
The price of each tool used and the shop it was bought from

questions.stem: Which is the best-written objective for a training session on safe isolation?
options: The trainee will understand all about isolation and why it matters
The trainee will prove a circuit dead, using every step, without help
The trainee will be shown many things about electricity during the day
The trainee will try hard to be a safer worker on site from now on

questions.stem: Why is on-the-job training best planned around real jobs the crew has coming up?
options: It means that no planning or paperwork is needed at all
It lets the contractor charge the client for training time
It means the trainee can work alone from the first day
The trainee practises real tasks in real site conditions

questions.stem: You have one week to train an apprentice in three new tasks. Which order is best?
options: From simple tasks to harder ones, building on each
From the hardest task first, to test them out early on
In any order, as long as all three are covered
In the order the materials arrive on site

questions.stem: Why should the training plan be agreed with your supervisor and the trainee?
options: So the supervisor can do the training instead
So the trainee can change the safety rules
So all know what will be learnt, when and with whom
So the plan does not have to be written down

questions.stem: You will teach a trainee to terminate a 220 V two-pole breaker. What should you prepare?
options: A live board, so the trainee can see the breaker working
A dead training board, tools, materials and the steps
Only a pen and paper, as the trainee will just watch you
A copy of the client's invoice for the job being done

questions.stem: On a busy building site, where is the best place to demonstrate a new task to a trainee?
options: A quiet, safe spot where they can see and hear you
Next to a running concrete mixer, so no time is lost
Up a ladder, so they see the job at its full height
In the site office, without the tools or materials

questions.stem: Why check the tools and test instruments before a training session starts?
options: So the trainee can see how old each one is
So the session can start later in the day
So the trainee will not need to touch them
So faulty items do not teach bad habits or cause harm

questions.stem: On a real job, what kind of electrical work may a trainee do?
options: Live work, if the supervisor is watching closely
Any work, once they have watched it done twice
Only dead work, under supervision, after safe isolation
Live testing at the main board on their own

questions.stem: You are showing a trainee how to prove a circuit dead. Which order is correct?
options: Check the tester on a known source, test the circuit, check the tester again
Test the circuit first, then check the tester on a known source once at the end
Check the tester once at the start of the day, then test all the circuits
Test the circuit with the tester, then touch the wires quickly to be sure

questions.stem: Why should a trainee fit their own padlock and tag when the crew isolates a circuit?
options: So the client knows the trainee's full name
So nobody can switch it on while they work on it
So the padlocks can be counted in the stores later
So the trainee learns the colour of each tag

questions.stem: A trainee is about to climb a mobile tower that has no guard rails fitted. What should you do?
options: Hold the tower yourself while they work quickly
Let them carry on and talk about it at break time
Tell them to keep one hand on the frame at all times
Stop them and have the tower put right before work

questions.stem: Why must the number of trainees one person supervises on site be kept small?
options: So each trainee can be watched and helped closely
So the trainees can all share one set of hand tools
So fewer training records need to be written
So the supervisor has time for other jobs

questions.stem: A trainee says he feels dizzy and sick while working in a hot roof space. What should you do first?
options: Tell him to finish the job quickly, then rest
Give him a cold drink and send him back up
Stop the work, get him somewhere cool and give water
Ask another trainee to take his place in the roof

questions.stem: Why should a trainee be shown the site's emergency procedure on their first day?
options: So they can leave the site early if the work is too hard
So they know how to raise the alarm and where to go
So they can explain it to the client later
So they can skip the safety induction

questions.stem: Which method is best for teaching a practical task such as crimping a cable lug?
options: Give them the maker's leaflet and let them work it out
Do it fast once, then ask them to repeat it from memory
Talk about it while they watch a different job
Explain it, show it, let them try it, then check it

questions.stem: When demonstrating a task, why do it first at normal speed and then again slowly, step by step?
options: It makes the session last longer
It shows how skilled the trainer is
They see the whole job, then each step clearly
It means the trainee need not practise

questions.stem: Where should the trainee stand while you demonstrate a termination at a board?
options: Facing you, so that they see all of the work back to front
Beside you, seeing it from the side they will work
Behind you, so that they are not in the way
Well back, as they only need to hear you

questions.stem: While demonstrating, why explain the reason for key steps, such as sleeving the bare earth conductor?
options: Knowing why helps them remember and apply it
It fills the time while you do the work
It means you can leave out the safety points
Trainees are not allowed to ask why

questions.stem: A task has 12 steps. How should you teach it to a new trainee?
options: Show all 12 steps once and expect them to remember
Teach only the last step, as it matters the most
Give them a written list and then leave them alone
Split it into small groups of steps and teach each

questions.stem: A trainee nods when you ask 'Do you understand?'. What is a better way to check?
options: Ask the same question again, more loudly
Ask them to explain or show the next step
Accept the nod and move on to the next task
Ask another trainee whether he understood

questions.stem: Which is an open question that checks a trainee's understanding?
options: Did you check the tester on the proving unit?
Is the circuit dead now that you tested it?
Why do we check the tester again after the test?
Are you ready to start the next part of the job?

questions.stem: Shanice reads English slowly and is shy about it. Which way of training helps her most?
options: Use pictures, short steps and showing her
Give her the full maker's manual to read at home
Speak faster so the session ends sooner
Leave her out of all the written work

questions.stem: Why should trade words such as 'CPC' or 'prove dead' be explained the first time you use them?
options: So the trainee can spell them in a test
So the session looks long and thorough
Trainees may not know them and may guess wrongly
So the client can follow the training too

questions.stem: After your demonstration, the trainee practises the task. What should you do?
options: Go to another job and come back to check later
Do the hard parts for them each time
Stand far away so they do not feel nervous
Watch closely and step in before any unsafe act

questions.stem: While stripping a cable, a trainee nicks the insulation of a conductor. What should happen?
options: Point out the nick, cut back and remake it properly
Cover the nick with insulating tape and carry on with the job
Leave it, as the cable will be hidden in the wall
Tell the trainee off in front of the whole crew

questions.stem: Why should a trainee practise a task several times before being assessed on it?
options: So the trainer has more time to do their own work
To build skill until it is right every time
So the crew can use up all the cable off-cuts
So the client can see how hard the crew works

questions.stem: A trainee has wired a two-way switching circuit on a training board. Which feedback is most useful?
options: Good job, that was fine, just carry on as you are
That was wrong, so you will have to do it again
Tight connections; next time label the strappers
You were slow compared with the other trainees

questions.stem: A trainee finished terminating a training board this morning. When should you give feedback on it?
options: Today, soon after the task, while it is fresh
At the end of the month, together with other jobs
Only at the final formal assessment
Only if the trainee asks for it

questions.stem: A trainee does a job well. Why should you tell them so?
options: So they will not need any more training
So they can be paid the same as an electrician
So you need not record it in the logbook
Praise builds confidence and keeps them trying

questions.stem: How can you best check that a trainee can now isolate a circuit safely?
options: Ask them whether they feel ready
Check that they have read the procedure
Watch them do it alone and ask why for each step
See whether they are faster than last time

questions.stem: A trainee did a task correctly once while you helped him. Is that enough to show he can do it?
options: Yes; one good try shows that he can do it
No; he must do it right on his own, more than once
Yes, as long as he says he understood it
No; he must first read the whole manual

questions.stem: After three sessions a trainee is still unsafe on ladders. What should you do?
options: Let them carry on, as they will improve with time
Remove them from the crew without telling anyone
Ask them to sign a note saying they will be careful
Report it, agree extra training, keep them off ladders

questions.stem: Why record each training session in the trainee's logbook or training record?
options: It shows what was learnt, when, and who checked it
It is used to work out the trainee's new rate of pay
It means the trainee will not be assessed later
It lets the client claim back the cost of the job

questions.stem: What should an entry in a trainee's training record include?
options: Only the trainee's name and the weather
The tools that were used and their prices
Date, task, standard reached, both signatures
Your own opinion of the trainee's family

questions.stem: Who should you tell when a trainee is falling behind the training plan?
options: The client, at the next weekly site meeting
Your supervisor or the training officer
The other trainees on the crew
Nobody, as it may upset the trainee

questions.stem: Why ask the trainee for their views at the end of a training session?
options: So the trainee can choose their final result
So you can find out who is to blame for any errors made
So the session can finish a little earlier
So you can improve the way you train next time

questions.stem: Two trainees on your crew come from different parishes, and one of them is a woman. How should you treat them in training?
options: Fairly and with respect, with the same chances
Give the man the harder tasks, as he will cope
Let them sort out their own training together
Give more help to the one from your own parish

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What kind of question cannot be answered with just 'yes' or 'no', and so makes a trainee explain?
What one word describes a trainee who can do a task safely, to the required standard, every time?
Finding the gap between what a worker can do now and what the job needs is called a training needs ______. Give the missing word.
What is the book or record called in which an apprentice's practical tasks are listed and signed off by the supervisor?
What do the letters OJT stand for, in workplace training?
A trainee learns best from diagrams, pictures and watching a demonstration. What is this learning style called?
A trainee learns best by doing the task with their own hands. What is this learning style called?
What one word means telling a trainee how well they did and what they should improve?
When a trainee locks off an isolator, what is fixed with the padlock to warn others, with their name and the date on it?
What one word names the part of a session in which the trainer shows how the task is done while the trainee watches?
What is the term for a statement of what the trainee will be able to do at the end of a session?
In competency-based training, what three-word result is given to a trainee who has not yet reached the standard?
What is it called when a job is split into small steps, written in order, so that each step can be taught in turn?
What is it called when a new worker follows an experienced worker through the day to watch how the job is done?
Which Jamaican national training agency manages the NVQ-J and the apprenticeship programmes?

essays.stem: Explain the role of an electrician who assists with on-the-job training on a crew. Say what they are responsible for and where their role ends.
essays.modelAnswer: An electrician who assists with on-the-job training helps a trainee learn real tasks safely while the work gets done. They help find out what the trainee can already do, agree a training plan with the supervisor, prepare the tools, materials and a safe place to train, and then explain and demonstrate each task. They watch the trainee practise, correct mistakes at once, give clear feedback and keep the trainee away from live work. They record each session in the logbook or training record and report progress, and any problems, to the supervisor or training officer. They must set a good example, because trainees copy what they see. Their role ends at the formal assessment: a qualified assessor decides whether the trainee is competent for the qualification. They also do not change the training plan or site rules on their own, and anything outside their skill or authority is passed to the supervisor.
markingPoints: Helps identify needs and plan training with the supervisor
Prepares, explains, demonstrates and supervises practice safely
Gives feedback and keeps records of each session
Reports progress and problems to the supervisor or training officer
States that the formal assessment is done by a qualified assessor

essays.stem: A school-leaver, Andre, has just joined your house-wiring crew in Portmore as an apprentice. Describe how you would find out what training he needs.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would talk with Andre and look at any certificates or records he brings, such as a Level 2 certificate or a logbook, to see what he has already learnt. I would ask him what tasks he has done before and which ones he feels unsure about. Next I would look at the tasks our crew does on house-wiring jobs, such as running cables, fixing boxes, terminating outlets and switches, safe isolation and reading the layout drawing, and the units of competency that cover them. Then I would watch him do a few simple, dead tasks on a training board, such as stripping and terminating a cable, to see his real skill and how he works safely. I would also ask how he likes to learn and whether reading is easy for him. Comparing what he can do with what the job needs shows the gap. I would write down the gap as a list of training needs, agree the order with my supervisor, and use it to make his training plan.
markingPoints: Checks his records, certificates and past experience
Lists the tasks the job needs, using the units of competency
Observes him doing simple dead tasks to see his real skill
Asks how he learns best, including reading
Writes down the gap and agrees it with the supervisor

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan a one-hour training session to teach a trainee the safe isolation procedure on a training board.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with a clear objective: by the end of the hour, the trainee will isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead a circuit on the training board, in the correct order, without help. I would write a short task breakdown with each step: identify the circuit, switch off, lock off with their own padlock, fit a tag, check the tester on a proving unit, test between all conductors, then check the tester again. I would book a dead training board that is never connected to a supply, and prepare the tester, proving unit, padlocks, tags and the written procedure with pictures. I would plan the time: about ten minutes to explain why each step matters, ten minutes to demonstrate, thirty minutes for the trainee to practise while I watch, and ten minutes to check understanding with open questions and give feedback. I would also plan how to record the session in the logbook and agree the plan with my supervisor beforehand.
markingPoints: States a clear, measurable objective
Lists the isolation steps in the correct order, including checking the tester before and after
Prepares a dead training board and the right equipment
Plans time for explaining, demonstrating, practice and checking
Plans the record and agrees the plan with the supervisor

essays.stem: Explain how you would demonstrate and teach a trainee to terminate a cable at a socket outlet, using the 'explain, demonstrate, practise, check' method.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would make sure the circuit is isolated and proved dead, or use a training board that has no supply. Explain: I would tell the trainee what we are doing and why, name the tools and parts, and point out the key safety and quality points, such as the correct strip length, no bare copper showing, sleeving the earth conductor and tight terminals. Demonstrate: with the trainee standing beside me, so they see it from the side they will work, I would terminate one outlet at normal speed, then again slowly, saying each step out loud. Practise: the trainee then terminates an outlet while I watch closely. I would let small slips be corrected straight away and stop anything unsafe. Check: I would inspect the work, ask open questions such as 'Why do we sleeve the earth?', and get them to do it again on their own. Finally I would give feedback and record the session.
markingPoints: Works dead: isolated and proved dead, or an unpowered training board
Explains the task, the tools and the key points first
Demonstrates at normal speed then slowly, with the trainee placed to see clearly
Lets the trainee practise under close supervision
Checks the work and understanding, gives feedback and records it

essays.stem: Explain how you would keep a trainee safe while they learn on a real electrical job site.
essays.modelAnswer: On the first day I would give the trainee the site induction: the hazards, the emergency procedure, the first-aid point and the site rules. I would check they have the right PPE, such as safety boots, a hard hat and eye protection, and know how to use it. The trainee would only do dead work, after the circuit is isolated, locked off with their own padlock, tagged and proved dead with a tester checked before and after use. They would never work live, and never test at a live board on their own. I would keep the number of trainees small, so I can watch each one closely, and stay with them when they use power tools or work at height, checking ladders and towers first. I would give short toolbox talks on the day's hazards, such as heat in roof spaces and sharp edges on trunking. If I saw an unsafe act, I would stop it at once, explain why and show the safe way, then report it if needed.
markingPoints: Induction, emergency procedure and PPE on the first day
Dead work only, with lock-off, tag and proving dead with a checked tester
Close supervision with a small number of trainees
Extra care with power tools and work at height
Stops unsafe acts at once, explains and reports

essays.stem: A trainee on your crew finds reading difficult and is embarrassed about it. Explain how you would adapt your training so that she still learns well.
essays.modelAnswer: I would speak with her privately and kindly, so she does not feel shamed, and agree the ways that help her most. I would rely more on showing and doing than on reading: demonstrate each task, let her practise, and check by watching her work and asking her to explain in her own words. I would use pictures, colour-coded diagrams, photos of each step and short notes with simple words and large print. Where a written procedure is needed, I would go through it with her, read it aloud and point to each step on the job. I would explain trade words when they first come up. I would check her understanding with open questions rather than written tests where I can, and keep sessions short. I would not leave her out of written work, but help her build her reading with simple job sheets. I would tell the supervisor, with her agreement, in case extra literacy support can be arranged.
markingPoints: Speaks privately and respectfully, without embarrassing her
Uses showing, doing and pictures more than reading
Uses simple words, explains trade terms and reads procedures with her
Checks understanding by observation and open questions
Arranges further support with the supervisor, with her agreement

essays.stem: Explain how to give useful feedback to a trainee after a practical task. Give an example from electrical work.
essays.modelAnswer: Useful feedback is given soon after the task, in private if it includes criticism, and is about the work, not the person. I would start by asking the trainee how they think it went, as this helps them learn to check their own work. Then I would say what was done well, using exact examples, so they keep doing it. Next I would name one or two things to improve, say why they matter and show how to do them. I would finish by agreeing the next step and encouraging them. For example, after a trainee wires a consumer unit on a training board: 'Your cable runs are neat and every terminal is tight, well done. Two points: two of the neutrals are not in the same order as their breakers, which makes fault-finding harder, and one earth is not sleeved. Let us look at how to fix these, then you do the next board on your own.' I would record the feedback in the training record.
markingPoints: Timely, private and about the work, not the person
Asks the trainee to review their own work first
Names exact strengths and one or two improvements, with reasons
Agrees the next step and encourages
Gives a suitable electrical example

essays.stem: Describe how you would check whether a trainee has learnt a task well enough to do it without close supervision, and what you would record.
essays.modelAnswer: I would check against the standard for the task, such as the unit of competency or the job's procedure. First I would watch the trainee do the whole task alone, without help or reminders, on dead work or a training board. I would look for the correct steps in the right order, safe working, the right tools and a finished result that meets the standard. I would ask open questions to check they understand why each step matters and what they would do if something went wrong, such as a tester failing on the proving unit. I would want to see it done right more than once, on different days or jobs, to be sure it is not luck. If the trainee meets the standard, I would record the date, the task, what I observed and the result, and both of us would sign the logbook. If not, I would record what still needs work and plan more practice. Final competence for the qualification is decided by the assessor.
markingPoints: Uses the task standard or unit of competency as the measure
Observes the trainee doing the whole task alone, safely
Asks questions to check understanding
Looks for consistent results over more than one attempt
Records date, task, result and signatures, and plans more practice if needed

essays.stem: A trainee keeps taking a shortcut: he does not check his tester on the proving unit before proving a circuit dead. Explain what you would do and why.
essays.modelAnswer: This is a serious safety matter, so I would deal with it at once and not let it pass. I would stop the work and speak to him privately and calmly. I would explain why the step matters: a tester that is faulty, has a flat battery or a broken lead can show 'dead' on a live circuit, and he could be killed or badly injured. Checking the tester on a proving unit before and after the test is the only way to know the result is true. I would ask him why he skips it, as there may be a reason, such as no proving unit in his kit or feeling rushed. I would demonstrate the correct steps again and have him repeat the full procedure correctly. I would record what happened and the extra training given. If it happens again, I would report it to the supervisor, as he must not do isolation work until he follows the procedure every time. I would also check that the crew sets the right example.
markingPoints: Stops the work at once and speaks to him privately
Explains the danger of a faulty tester showing dead on a live circuit
Finds out the reason for the shortcut
Retrains and has him repeat the full procedure correctly
Records it and reports to the supervisor if it happens again

essays.stem: Explain how you would find out whether the on-the-job training you helped to give was effective, and how you would use what you found.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first look at the objectives in the training plan and check whether the trainee can now do each task to the standard, by watching their work and reading the training record. I would look at work results, such as how often their work passes the supervisor's inspection first time, and whether they work safely without reminders. I would ask the trainee for their views: what helped them learn, what was hard and what could be done better. I would also ask the supervisor and other crew members what they see on the job. Then I would compare what was planned with what happened, such as tasks that took longer to learn or methods that did not work. I would use what I found to change the next training: for example more practice time, more pictures and fewer written notes, or a better place to demonstrate. I would report the results to the supervisor and agree any changes to the training plan.
markingPoints: Checks results against the training objectives
Uses work results and safe working as evidence
Gets the trainee's views and the supervisor's or crew's views
Identifies what worked and what did not
Uses the findings to improve the next training and reports them

practical1.title: Plan and deliver a short on-the-job demonstration of safe isolation on a dead training board
practical1.brief: Your group plans and delivers a training session in which an experienced worker teaches a new apprentice the safe isolation procedure. The assessor gives you a training board that is never connected to a supply, with a lockable isolator. As a group, first write a one-page session plan: the objective, the task breakdown (each step in order), the equipment, the safety points, the timing and how understanding will be checked. Then take turns: each member acts as the trainer for one part of the session (explaining, demonstrating, supervising practice, questioning, or giving feedback), while another member plays the apprentice and the rest observe and complete an observation sheet. The trainer for the practice part watches the 'apprentice' isolate, lock off, tag and prove the circuit dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. At the end, the group fills in a training record entry for the apprentice and writes three improvements to the session. Every member must deliver at least one part and complete at least one observation sheet. Photograph each stage below.
materials: Training board with a lockable isolator, never connected to a supply
Approved voltage tester and proving unit
Padlocks, lock-off devices and 'Danger – do not switch on' tags
Blank session plan, task breakdown, observation sheet and training record forms
Picture cards of each isolation step (made by the group or supplied)
photos: The completed session plan and task breakdown
The trainer explaining and demonstrating, with the apprentice placed to see clearly
The apprentice proving the tester on the proving unit, testing, and proving it again
The lock and tag fitted by the apprentice
Completed observation sheets from the observers
The training record entry and the list of improvements
checklist: Helped write a clear, measurable objective and correct task breakdown
Delivered their part of the session clearly, using plain words
Demonstrated or checked the isolation steps in the correct order
Used open questions to check understanding
Gave feedback that named strengths and an improvement
Kept the session safe and treated the 'apprentice' with respect
safety: The training board is never connected to a supply; only the instructor may energise anything at the Centre
Treat the board as if it could be live: follow the full isolation and proving steps every time
Check the tester and leads for damage before use
Keep the work area tidy and keep bags and leads off the floor

practical2.title: Prepare a two-week on-the-job training pack for a new apprentice and role-play a progress review
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a short profile of a new apprentice joining an electrical crew that is wiring a small block of apartments in Spanish Town, and a list of the crew's tasks for the next two weeks. As a group, prepare a training pack. Share the roles: one member writes a training needs checklist comparing what the apprentice can do with what the job needs; one writes a two-week training plan (task, objective, trainer, day and how it will be checked); two members each write a job breakdown sheet, with simple words and sketches, for one task (for example fixing and wiring a switch box, and terminating a cable at a two-pole breaker on a dead board); and one designs a logbook page and a feedback form. The group checks each other's work and puts the pack together. Then role-play an end-of-week progress review: one member plays the apprentice (using the assessor's role card), one plays the workplace trainer giving feedback and agreeing next steps, and one plays the supervisor; the others take notes. Swap roles so every member speaks at least once. Photograph each stage below.
materials: Apprentice profile and two-week task list (supplied by the assessor)
Role cards for the progress review (supplied by the assessor)
Blank training plan, job breakdown, logbook and feedback forms
Copies of the relevant unit standards or task procedures
Flip-chart paper, rulers, markers and pens
photos: Each job breakdown sheet with its sketches
The logbook page and feedback form
The progress review role play, at each change of roles
The review notes and the agreed next steps
checklist: Completed their own part of the pack clearly and accurately
Matched training to the gaps shown in the needs checklist
Wrote steps in a logical order, with safety points and dead working
Used plain words and pictures suitable for a trainee
